title: Hundred Grid Shader
context: Grade 5, the pages on hundredths and thousandths. An adult sees two more fractions with bigger denominators. What the pages are doing is cutting each part into ten again: a tenth into hundredths, a hundredth into thousandths. The exercise that says figures means drawn grids, and any squares of the right number are correct.

writeup.why: Read and shade hundredths on a hundred grid, writing them as fractions and as decimals, and see thousandths come from cutting a hundredth into ten.
writeup.look: A full ten by ten grid at the left, the Columns and squares counter under it, a fraction card and a decimal card at its right, and a zoomed square on the last phase.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Hundred Grid Shader' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many squares are shaded, rising as the child drags and falling as it clears. On the last phase it counts thin slices instead. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The grid is 480 by 480 at x 110, y 226, ten columns of ten squares, every square 48 across, ruled in near-black and labelled Whole above its top edge. Shaded squares are deep blue; unshaded squares stay warm white. The lifted column stands at x 640, y 226, its ten squares spread with small gaps, labelled 1 tenth above and 1 hundredth on its top square. The Columns and squares counter sits under the grid at y 716 in ink. The fraction card and the decimal card stand at x 900, y 300, one above the other, turning green when the child's answer matches the shading. On the last phase the zoomed square is drawn as a strip 400 long and 60 tall at x 640, y 520, cut into ten thin slices by near-black lines, each labelled 1 thousandth, with a fine line back to the square it came from. The Cut column, Scatter and Zoom buttons sit in a row at x 640, y 440. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key and a fraction bar key, for setting a number of hundredths or thousandths, or for typing a fraction or a decimal into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last grid beside its fraction over 100 and its decimal, with one square lifted and sliced into thousandths.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the child taps Scatter, the shaded squares lift off the grid, drift about like leaves and settle in new places, and the decimal card stays exactly as it was.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with the grid in place. On the first phase the grid is empty with one column outlined in amber and the words one tenth above it. On the second a shading is already on the grid and the Columns and squares counter is hidden. On the third the grid is empty and the question card names a number of hundredths. On the fourth one square is outlined in amber and the Zoom button is lit. One thing moves, once: the outlined column or square, or the grid's first square, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any shading of the grid, scattered or in columns, and any square zoomed and sliced. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on hundredths of a tenth, reading and shading grids, and thousandths.

source_tool.description: A full ten by ten grid, 480 by 480, sits at the left of the working area, labelled Whole, with its ten columns ruled in near-black and every square the same size. A Cut column button lifts one column out beside the grid and splits it into its ten squares, with the words 1 tenth above the column and 1 hundredth on one square. Dragging across squares shades them deep blue; dragging back clears them. A Columns and squares counter under the grid reads the shading as full columns of ten and single squares, and a fraction card and a decimal card to the right give it as hundredths, turning green when the child's answer matches. A Scatter button moves the shaded squares to other places on the grid while their number stays the same, and the cards stay as they were. On the last phase a Zoom button lifts one square up to the size of a strip and cuts it into ten thin equal slices, each labelled 1 thousandth, and a Thousandths tally counts the slices shaded. A number pad sets any number of hundredths up to one hundred, or any number of thousandths. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many squares are shaded.
source_tool.art_direction: Squared paper, ten by ten / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the full columns first, then the single squares.
voice.onNext: A new grid. Count by columns of ten.
voice.opening: A hundred small squares, all the same size.
voice.onFinish: Tenths into hundredths, and hundredths into thousandths.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Shade, scatter and zoom as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has cut one tenth of a paper square into ten thin strips and drawn a hundred grid on squared paper. The tool is what moves the shading about without changing its count, and what cuts one square into ten, which paper cannot do at a size a child can see.

answer_key.rule: A tenth cut into ten equal parts gives hundredths, so 10 hundredths make 1 tenth and a hundred grid holds 100 hundredths. Count full columns of ten first, then single squares, and write the count over 100, or with two digits after the point. To show a number of hundredths, shade any squares of that count: which squares does not matter, only how many. A hundredth cut into ten equal parts gives thousandths, so 10 thousandths make 1 hundredth.
answer_key.wrong: The grid is shown again with the shaded squares counted column by column, a number on each full column and on each single square, and the child's answer is shaded on a second grid beside it, so the two counts are seen side by side. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The grid has 100 equal squares, so each square is one hundredth.
So one column is 10 hundredths, and 1/10 = 10/100.
items.question: One column of a hundred grid is one tenth of the grid. How many hundredths is one column?
items.misconception: Saying one column is one hundredth, which counts the column as a single square.

steps: Each full column is 10 squares, so 5 columns are 50 squares.
53 of the 100 squares are shaded, so the fraction is 53/100.
Hundredths take two digits after the point, so 53/100 = 0.53.
items.question: A hundred grid has 5 full columns and 3 more squares shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction and as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: Count full columns of ten first, then the single squares.
items.misconception: Writing 5.3 because 5 columns and 3 squares were counted, which reads the columns as wholes.

steps: Shade any 4 squares of the 100. Which ones does not matter, only how many.
items.question: Shade a hundred grid to show 0.04.
items.checkpoint: Any squares of the right count show a number of hundredths.
items.misconception: Shading 4 full columns, 40 squares, which shows 0.4, ten times as much.

steps: The whole holds 100 hundredths, and each is cut into 10, so the whole holds 1000 equal parts.
3 parts are shaded, so the fraction is 3/1000.
Thousandths take three digits after the point, so 3/1000 = 0.003.
items.question: One hundredth is cut into 10 equal parts and 3 of them are shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction and as a decimal.
items.misconception: Writing 0.03 for three thousandths, which is 3 hundredths, ten times as much.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many hundredths make one tenth?
A hundred grid has 6 full columns shaded and nothing else. Write the shaded part as a decimal.
items.final_answer: 60 of the 100 squares, 60/100, which is 0.60 or 0.6

items.question: How many squares of a hundred grid do you shade to show 0.21?
A hundred grid has 2 full columns and 9 more squares shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction and as a decimal.
How many squares do you shade to show 0.3, and how many to show 0.03?
How many thousandths make one hundredth?
Write 41 thousandths as a fraction and as a decimal.
Two children show 0.14 on hundred grids. One shades a full column and 4 more squares. The other shades 14 squares scattered about. Who is right?
items.final_answer: Both are right. Each shaded 14 of the 100 squares, and which squares does not matter

teaching_notes: Cut one tenth of a paper square into ten thin strips before the tool opens, and lay one beside the whole square. Count full columns of ten first and single squares after. Any squares of the right count are correct, so accept a scattered shading as readily as a tidy one; the exercise that says figures means a drawn grid. Put six hundredths beside six tenths on two grids so the zero after the point is seen to matter. Draw every grid as a full ten by ten.
generation_prompt: Build a hundredths tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A full ten by ten grid, 480 by 480, sits at the left of the working area, labelled Whole. A Cut column button lifts one column out and splits it into its ten squares, labelled 1 tenth and 1 hundredth. Dragging shades squares deep blue. A Columns and squares counter reads the shading as full columns and single squares, and a fraction card and a decimal card give it as hundredths, turning green when the answer matches. A Scatter button moves the shaded squares without changing their number. On the last phase a Zoom button lifts one square to strip size and cuts it into ten thin slices, each labelled 1 thousandth. A number pad sets hundredths or thousandths. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of shaded squares. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right.
